queries.hyde_abstract: Educational agents must adapt to learners’ knowledge, goals, preferences, pace and affect while maintaining coherent interactions over extended learning activities. We present a personalized agentic tutoring system that combines a learner model, long-term interaction memory, retrieval over instructional resources and planning tools for generating adaptive explanations, exercises and feedback. The agent updates its estimate of student mastery from dialogue, answers and learning behaviors, and selects actions according to both pedagogical objectives and learner preferences. We evaluate the system with students across varied prior knowledge and compare it with non-personalized tutoring and static conversational assistance. Personalization improves learning gains, engagement and task completion, particularly for students with heterogeneous misconceptions, but errors in learner-state estimation can lead to inappropriate scaffolding. Ablation studies show that explicit pedagogical planning and calibrated memory are important for reliable adaptation.

queries.bm25_query: evaluation personalized agentic systems education educational agents intelligent tutoring learning gains personalization quality pedagogical effectiveness student engagement fairness safety
queries.hyde_abstract: Evaluating personalized educational agents requires measuring more than conversational fluency or immediate task success. We propose a framework that jointly assesses learning gains, retention, personalization quality, pedagogical appropriateness, interaction experience, equity and safety. The framework combines pretest-posttest learning measures, delayed assessments, expert ratings of instructional decisions, student judgments of adaptation, interaction logs and analyses of differential performance across learner groups. In a controlled study, personalized agents produce larger short-term gains than generic agents, but improvements in perceived helpfulness do not always predict retention. We further find that agents can over-personalize by lowering challenge for struggling students and can perform unevenly across language backgrounds. We recommend reporting learner-level outcomes, longitudinal measures and subgroup analyses alongside standard automatic and human evaluations.

queries.hyde_abstract: Deep research agents must go beyond single-step retrieval by decomposing complex questions, searching heterogeneous sources, verifying evidence, and synthesizing findings into coherent reports. We present a modular agent architecture that combines query planning, iterative web search, document reading, evidence tracking, and citation-aware generation. The agent maintains a structured research graph linking claims to supporting passages and revises its search strategy when evidence is incomplete or contradictory. We compare fixed pipelines with adaptive tool-using agents across multi-hop, temporal and synthesis-oriented research questions. Adaptive planning improves source coverage and citation completeness, particularly for questions requiring several dependent searches, while uncontrolled browsing increases cost and exposes the system to irrelevant or low-quality sources. Ablation studies show that explicit evidence tracking and claim-level verification are central to reliable deep research.

queries.hyde_abstract: Evaluating deep research agents requires more than judging the quality of their final reports. We introduce a component-level evaluation framework that separately measures question decomposition, search quality, document selection, evidence extraction, claim verification, citation correctness, synthesis, and computational cost. The framework combines process traces with reference-supported annotations and evaluates both intermediate decisions and final answers on complex research questions. We find that report-level factuality can conceal substantial retrieval and attribution failures: agents may produce plausible summaries while relying on incomplete or weakly relevant evidence. Retrieval recall and citation entailment are the strongest predictors of answer reliability, whereas longer reports are not consistently better. Component ablations and error analyses show that diagnostic evaluation provides more actionable insights than aggregate answer scores for improving deep research agents.

queries.hyde_abstract: Hallucinations—confidently generated statements that are unsupported or false—remain a central limitation of large language models. Across question answering, summarization and open-ended generation, we compare internal confidence, token entropy, retrieval evidence and memorization estimates. Hallucinations are most common when prompts require compositional inference beyond memorized facts, when the input distribution differs from pretraining data, and when decoding favors fluent but weakly supported continuations. Our analysis suggests that hallucination is a heterogeneous phenomenon arising from interactions between data coverage, model representations and generation dynamics rather than from a single defect.

Results show that effective post-training depends on matching the learning signal to the domain agent’s interaction structure.

Long-context models perform well when evidence is dense, references are distributed across the input, or reasoning requires global document structure. However, accuracy declines when relevant evidence is sparse, repeated distractors increase attention demands, and inference cost becomes substantial. Our analysis shows that nominal context-window size is a poor proxy for usable context and identifies workload characteristics favoring direct long-context processing.

aspects.name: Retrieval-augmented generation
aspects.description: Papers that use retrieval-augmented generation to supply LLM systems with relevant external information instead of placing all available information in the context. They examine when retrieval improves answer quality, efficiency, factuality, and adaptation to changing knowledge.

queries.hyde_abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation reduces the input burden on LLM systems by selecting a small set of passages from a larger corpus before generation. We investigate when RAG is preferable to processing an entire source collection with a long-context model. Across document question answering, knowledge-intensive dialogue and temporally changing information, retrieval improves efficiency and factuality when relevant evidence is sparse and the corpus is large. Its benefits diminish when questions require synthesis across many dispersed passages or when the retriever fails to identify the needed evidence. We compare dense retrieval, hybrid search and reranking under fixed latency budgets. Results show that retrieval quality and evidence coverage, rather than context-window length alone, determine the usefulness of RAG, while retrieval errors remain its dominant failure mode.

aspects.name: Explicit memory mechanisms
aspects.description: Papers that equip LLM systems with explicit memory mechanisms, such as structured memories, episodic memories, summaries, or external stores, to retain information across interactions or tasks. They study when persistent memory is preferable to repeatedly using long contexts or retrieving from an unstructured corpus.

queries.hyde_abstract: Explicit memory mechanisms allow LLM systems to retain and organize information across interactions rather than repeatedly processing complete conversation histories. We study episodic memories, compressed summaries and structured user profiles for long-term dialogue and personalized assistance. The system extracts candidate memories, assigns provenance and recency metadata, and retrieves or updates them when future turns require prior information. Compared with unrestricted conversation-history prompting and document retrieval, explicit memory improves consistency on recurring preferences and enables lower inference cost over long sessions. Its weaknesses include incorrect memory formation, stale facts and unwanted retention of irrelevant or sensitive details. Evaluations measuring recall, contradiction rate, personalization and memory-editing behavior show that explicit memory is most useful for persistent, user-specific information rather than one-off factual questions.

aspects.name: Choosing context strategies
aspects.description: Papers that directly compare long-context models, retrieval-augmented generation, and explicit memory mechanisms for LLM systems. They identify workload, evidence, latency, cost, update frequency, and persistence conditions that determine when each strategy should be used.

queries.hyde_abstract: LLM system designers must choose among long-context processing, retrieval-augmented generation and explicit memory, yet these mechanisms are often evaluated in isolation. We present a controlled comparison across workloads differing in corpus size, evidence dispersion, update frequency, session length and personalization requirements. Long-context models are strongest when the relevant information is distributed throughout a moderate-sized source and global interactions matter. RAG offers the best cost-quality trade-off for large, searchable and frequently updated collections, but suffers from retrieval misses. Explicit memory is superior for stable user-specific information that must persist across sessions, while requiring safeguards against stale or incorrect memories. Hybrid systems that retrieve documents and maintain compact memories perform best overall, suggesting that strategy selection should be based on information structure rather than context-window capacity alone.
